Issued at 138 PM EDT Sat Oct 10 2026

*** BREEZY WITH RAIN SHOWERS THROUGH SUNDAY ***

The remnants of Isaias are bringing portions of southern and central 
Kentucky beneficial rain early Saturday afternoon, while winds 
steadily increase out of the east-northeast. Thankfully, gusts have 
generally stayed in the 20-30 mph range so far, though a few have 
reached 35 mph just to our south in central Tennessee - running on 
the low end of HREF guidance as is often the case in warm advection 
regimes characterized by stable low levels. Given a notable LLJ - 
evident via 50-55 kt winds at just 1kft AGL off of HPX's VAD - 
lifting north across the area this evening, there remains a low 
chance that momentum transfer via heavier showers could mix down a 
rogue 40+ mph gust, but Bufkit soundings from various models suggest 
this would be brief and localized, with the risk decreasing sharply 
after 7-8pm EDT as the low level inversion strengthens. Hence, we 
don't anticipate needing a Wind Advisory at this time, but opted to 
continue the Special Weather Statement (SPS) through 7pm EDT 
mentioning the low chance of minor impacts like lightweight, outdoor 
objects blowing around.

Otherwise, scattered showers will continue overnight, with perhaps a 
rumble of thunder or two this evening as MUCAPE, just barely poking 
into the dendritic growth zone (DGZ) for charge separation, reaches 
300-500 J/kg - highest over the Bluegrass. We'll keep an extra eye 
on radar during the evening, but the chance for severe weather is 
exceptionally low.

The surface low will pivot over eastern Kentucky tomorrow, resulting 
in lingering showers mainly over the Bluegrass. Though we may see a 
few peaks of sunshine during the afternoon mainly west of I-65, the 
low will have "filled" (weakened) considerably by that time so winds 
will be relatively light. This position of the low to our east 
should also reduce the risk for cold air funnels and/or a landspout, 
with the RAP/NAM both showing highest (>1) non-supercell tornado 
parameters (NSTs) in far eastern Kentucky and parts of West 
Virginia, though our risk remains nonzero. Any showers will be slow-
moving, so there could be some localized pockets of moderate-heavy 
rainfall (again, most likely over the Bluegrass) exceeding 1.5 
inches, but this is not anticipated to cause any hydrological 
impacts given 6 hour Flash Flood Guidance (FFG), or the minimum 
amount of rainfall required to cause flooding, is running 3-4 inches 
due to the dry antecedent conditions. Due to the showery nature of 
the precipitation this evening and again tomorrow afternoon, 
rainfall totals will vary considerably from one location to another. 
HREF/NBM 10th-90th percentile ranges for storm totals span less than 
a quarter inch to more than 2 in spots, with high end amounts 
running highest over the Bluegrass. Rain should finally taper off 
tomorrow evening as dry air works in from the northwest behind the 
low. High temperatures tomorrow will, like today, struggle to 
surpass 70, which is near normal for mid October.

*** DRY MONDAY-TUESDAY, RAIN CHANCES RETURN MIDWEEK ***

We may kick off the work week with some fog early Monday morning if 
clouds break up, since surface high pressure will be over the area 
resulting in light winds. The 12z HRRR is certainly advertising the 
potential with sub quarter-mile visibilities near/east of the I-75 
corridor. We'll monitor trends in cloud cover and winds to reassess 
that potential, but for now we'll hold off on a key message about 
the fog, which has been added to the gridded forecast east of 
roughly I-65. Global models and their ensembles are in agreement 
that ridging will build back over the Ohio Valley on Monday, with 
southwest surface winds and deep mixing bringing temperatures back 
into the mid 80s during the afternoon - about 15 degrees warmer than 
Sunday. Tuesday will be similarly warm, though becoming less dry as 
Gulf moisture, lifted into the Plains on Monday, slowly spills into 
our area from the west. The GFS and ECMWF then each depict a 
southern stream shortwave ejecting out of the Southern/Central 
Plains and into the Illinois/Indiana sometime Wednesday into 
Thursday, which forecast soundings suggest will result in some 
elevated instability and (conditional on a trigger) some chance for 
showers and thunderstorms. At this time, the National Blend of 
Models (NBM) gives the area a 20-40% chance for rain Wednesday into 
Thursday. The jury's out on how things will evolve at the end of the 
week, with EOF patterns (specifically PC1 for EOF1) for 500mb height 
suggesting model spread in the depth of troughing over the Upper 
Midwest/Great Lakes is the primary driver of uncertainty during the 
Friday-Saturday timeframe. This may be related to the deterministic 
models, which have portrayed various outcomes with potential 
interaction between a cutoff low over the Four Corners and a series 
of systems rippling through the northern stream jet.
